title: Telehealth is Crucial for Women's Health
subtitle: A call to action, with Joanna Strober of Midi Health
body_html:
I’m a huge fan of appropriate regulations—and those who advocate for making them ever more relevant to the care of patients. Today’s column is a gI’m also a huge fan of Joanna Strober—she is the founder of Midi Health, which provides excellent Telehealth care for women in midlife. Her blog is available here. She authored this call to action to let our colleagues at DEA know what kinds of care are on the line when addressing controlled substances. Joanna…take it away!

Share

All of Midi’s care is delivered via our virtual care platform. We are serving over 100K women and all of them require a variety of medications, from hormone replacement therapy to naltraoxone.


Being a virtual provider is crucial because it breaks down the barriers to quality care. We’re able to reach women who might otherwise miss out on menopause care, whether due to geographic or financial limitations, busy schedules, or simply because— after years of being bounced around from doctor to doctor—they don’t have the energy to book and travel to yet another appointment.

Now, thanks to telehealth, women can get empathetic, expert midlife care and prescription treatments from the comfort of their couch—covered by insurance. It’s a simple but life-changing concept. And it’s in jeopardy.

A new proposal from the Drug Enforcement Agency threatens to limit the ability to prescribe controlled substances via telemedicine.

If finalized, it would severely hurt the telehealth industry that took off during the pandemic, but more importantly, it would hurt women.

Many controlled substances are medications that women rely on to feel their best and protect their health during menopause—and every other stage of life.

These medications include anxiolytics and sleep aids, like Ativan and Lunesta. Women experience higher rates of anxiety disorders and insomnia, and prescriptions like these give them some relief. Gabapentin, which is crucial for managing hot flashes and sleep issues, especially for breast cancer survivors who can’t take hormonal treatments, would be affected. As would Suboxone, which is used to treat opioid dependence, a disorder that disproportionately affects women.

Telehealth access to this medication is vital for women seeking addiction treatment, especially those in rural areas with limited access to in-person care.

The list goes on and on, but the point is: Access to telehealth prescribing is no longer a novelty, it’s a necessity for the well-being of society.

We started a petition, urging the DEA to extend prescribing flexibilities. We invite you to sign it, share it, and get loud about the damaging effects this proposal would have to women.

Here is the petition.

It is an honor to have Joanna join The Frontier Psychiatrists for some much needed gravitas around this crucial issue.
